name: singapore
title: Singapore
note: About 2,300 mm of rain a year in short, intense convective bursts. The interesting case for this product: Singapore has one of the best drainage networks in the world, and we have no drainage data for it at all. Our screening should therefore overstate pooling here more than anywhere else — which is exactly the limit we disclose on every run, now visible rather than theoretical.

terrain.source: DeltaDTM v1.1 (Pronk et al. 2024), via Earth Engine community catalog
terrain.note: Raw band. Non-finite is sea or outside coverage; the value 30 is the model's cap.

population.note: Total population placed by a modelled grid. The census check is of residents only, so the dormitory workers in the published total are spread like residents. An order of magnitude for who is exposed, by area.

news_query: Singapore (flood OR flooding OR "flash flood" OR "heavy rain" OR ponding OR waterlogging)

heat_standard.incomplete: The wet-bulb globe temperature needs solar radiation, which the hourly forecast does not carry. This product never converts a forecast into it. Where a WBGT figure appears it is a reading NEA took, not our estimate.

surface_heat.source: Landsat 8 and 9 Collection 2 Level 2 surface temperature (USGS), via Earth Engine
surface_heat.licence: USGS Landsat data are public domain
surface_heat.season: all months of the year, as Singapore has no dry season
surface_heat.composite: median of every clear view; cloud, cirrus, shadow and water masked
surface_heat.resolution: the thermal sensor resolves patches about 100 m across; USGS delivers it resampled to a 30 m grid, and this is on the terrain's 1 arcsec grid
surface_heat.grid: the staged terrain's own 1 arcsec grid, nearest neighbour from Landsat's 30 m
surface_heat.unit: degrees C of the SURFACE, not the air
caveats: A typical-season picture, not a forecast and not today.
Surface temperature, the skin of roofs, roads and leaves. In sun it runs well above air temperature and is not comparable with a forecast figure.
Landsat passes at mid-morning. Afternoon surfaces run hotter and spread further apart.
The thermal sensor sees patches about 100 m across, so this shows a few blocks at best and never a single building or roof.
Water is masked: this is a picture of land.

population_grid.source: GHS-POP R2023A, 2020 epoch, 100 m population count (European Commission JRC), via Earth Engine
population_grid.resolution: 100 m equal-area source, resampled through people per square metre onto a 3 arcsecond (about 93 m) lat/lon grid; a modelled estimate, not a head count
population_grid.unit: people per pixel (a count, not a density)
caveats: A modelled estimate of where people live, at about 100 m. It is not a head count.
Scaled so the staged area adds up to the published figure: the grid says where, the census says how many.

Inside a spot, people are placed on the mapped buildings in their cell, so a spot over open ground holds nobody. Where a cell has people and no mapped building they are spread evenly over the cell instead.

validation.against: Singapore Census of Population 2020, resident population by planning area (SingStat, via data.gov.sg), with Master Plan 2019 planning area boundaries
validation.judged_on: each method's share of the city in each planning area, so where people are placed and not how many
validation.caveat: The census counts residents only (about 4.0 million of about 5.9 million people), so dormitory workers are missing from the truth and no method can score perfectly.

hazard.source: GEM Global Seismic Hazard Map v2023.1 (Johnson et al. 2023), GEM Foundation
hazard.quantity: peak ground acceleration, as a fraction of g
hazard.exceedance: 10% chance of being exceeded in 50 years (the 475-year level)
hazard.native_res: 3 arcminute grid (about 5.5 km), interpolated from points about 6 km apart

ground.source: USGS global hybrid Vs30 mosaic (Heath, Wald, Worden, Thompson and Smoczyk 2020)
ground.quantity: Vs30, the average shear-wave speed of the top 30 m, in m/s
ground.method: topographic slope (Allen and Wald 2007) as the default, regional maps inserted where they exist

seismic.amplification: Borcherdt (1994) short-period factors, in the form and values USGS tabulate in Open-File Report 2007-1357, Table 1
seismic.intensity: Worden et al. (2012) peak-ground-acceleration relation, as USGS ShakeMap implements it
caveats: The published design-level shaking: the level with a one in ten chance of being exceeded in fifty years. It is a hazard level, not a forecast and not an earthquake.
The ground is estimated from the shape of the land at about 900 m. In a flat city almost everything looks alike to that method, and it cannot see a pocket of soft clay or made ground.
No data on what buildings stand here or how they are built is held, so nothing here says anything about damage, injury or death.
